title: Signals, bandwidth and channel capacity
subtitle: Any signal is a sum of sine waves. How many you need is its bandwidth, and bandwidth plus noise sets the speed limit.

sections.title: Sine waves and the frequency domain
sections.body:
Start with the simplest wiggle in nature: a pendulum swinging back and forth. A periodic signal has a period T, the time of one swing, and a frequency f = 1/T, the swings per second. A sine wave A sin(2πft + φ) is described by exactly three things: amplitude, frequency and phase.

There are two ways to look at a signal. The time domain shows amplitude against time; the frequency domain shows how much of each frequency is present. Do one: a signal repeats every 20 ms, so T = 20 ms and f = 1/T = 50 Hz. A sine wave with a period of 4 ms has f = 250 Hz. Try it yourself.

questions.prompt: A sine wave has period 4 ms. Its frequency?

keynotes: A periodic signal has period T and frequency f = 1/T; a sine wave A sin(2πft + φ) has amplitude, frequency and phase.
The time domain shows amplitude against time; the frequency domain shows how much of each frequency is present.
A signal repeating every 20 ms has f = 1/T = 50 Hz.

sections.title: Fourier series
sections.body:
Here is one of the most beautiful ideas in engineering. Fourier showed that any periodic signal is a sum of sine waves at multiples (harmonics) of its fundamental frequency. Even a sharp-cornered square wave is built from smooth sines: sin x + ⅓ sin 3x + ⅕ sin 5x + … (odd harmonics only).

Step through the figure and watch the edges sharpen as you add harmonics. The RMS error falls from 0.315 with 3 harmonics to 0.1 with 49. Yet notice a stubborn ripple at each jump that never disappears: the Gibbs phenomenon. So which harmonics does a square wave contain? Only the odd ones.

questions.prompt: A square wave contains which harmonics?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Its symmetry cancels the even ones.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Then it would be a sine.

figures.caption: Figure 2.2.1 — building a square wave
figures.note: Step through: more harmonics, sharper edges.

keynotes: Any periodic signal is a sum of sine waves at multiples (harmonics) of its fundamental frequency.
A square wave is sin x + ⅓ sin 3x + ⅕ sin 5x + … (odd harmonics only).
The RMS error falls from 0.315 with 3 harmonics to 0.1 with 49, but a ripple at each jump never disappears (the Gibbs phenomenon).

sections.title: Bandwidth
sections.body:
If a signal is a bundle of sine waves, how wide is the bundle? The bandwidth of a signal is the range of frequencies it occupies. A channel passes only a band, so sharp-edged signals, which need many harmonics, get their corners rounded off by a narrow channel.

To send a square wave reasonably you need at least the 3rd–5th harmonic: for a 1 kHz square wave, about 5 kHz. Test a case: a 2 kHz square wave through a channel that passes 0–8 kHz. Which harmonics get through? Odd harmonics up to 8 kHz: 2 and 6 kHz (the 3rd). The 10 kHz (5th) is cut off. A narrow channel loses the high harmonics that make the corners, so the square wave is rounded.

worked.why: Send a 2 kHz square wave through a channel that passes 0–8 kHz. Which harmonics get through?
Odd harmonics up to 8 kHz: 2, 6 kHz (3rd). 10 kHz (5th) is cut off.

questions.prompt: Why does a narrow-bandwidth channel round off a square wave?

choices.text: It removes the high harmonics that make the edges sharp.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Sharp edges are made of high frequencies.

keynotes: The bandwidth of a signal is the range of frequencies it occupies.
Sharp-edged signals need many harmonics, so a narrow channel rounds them off; a 1 kHz square wave needs about 5 kHz.
A 2 kHz square wave through a 0–8 kHz channel passes 2 and 6 kHz and loses the 10 kHz harmonic.

sections.title: Nyquist and Shannon capacity
sections.body:
Is there a speed limit for a wire? Yes, two of them, from two clever people. Nyquist (noiseless): max bit rate = 2B log₂ M for bandwidth B and M signal levels. Shannon (noisy): capacity C = B log₂(1 + SNR), with SNR as a ratio (dB = 10 log₁₀ ratio). Nyquist says more levels give more bits; Shannon says noise puts a ceiling on how many levels you can tell apart, however clever the coding.

Let’s use them on a 3 kHz telephone channel with SNR 30 dB. 30 dB is a ratio of 10³ = 1000, so Shannon gives C = 3000 log₂(1001) ≈ 29 900 b/s. How many levels would Nyquist need to reach that? 2B log₂M = 6000 log₂M, so log₂ M ≈ 4.98 and M ≈ 32. If you double the bandwidth while the SNR stays fixed, the capacity doubles too.

worked.why: A 3 kHz telephone channel, SNR 30 dB.
Levels needed under Nyquist to reach that (2B log₂M = 6000 log₂M): log₂ M ≈ 4.98 → M ≈ 32.

questions.prompt: Doubling the bandwidth while the SNR stays fixed…

problems.prompt: A channel has 4 kHz bandwidth and SNR of 15 (ratio). Find the Shannon capacity.
A noiseless 6 kHz channel carries 8-level signals. Maximum data rate?

keynotes: Nyquist (noiseless): maximum bit rate = 2B log₂ M for bandwidth B and M signal levels.
Shannon (noisy): capacity C = B log₂(1 + SNR), with dB = 10 log₁₀ ratio; noise puts a ceiling on distinguishable levels.
A 3 kHz channel at 30 dB (ratio 1000) has capacity of about 29 900 b/s, which Nyquist reaches with about 32 levels.

sections.title: Sampling: the Nyquist rate
sections.body:
To put a voice into a computer you must turn the smooth wave into numbers by sampling it, taking snapshots. How fast? At least twice per cycle of its highest frequency (fs ≥ 2 fmax). Take fewer and something sneaky happens: higher frequencies masquerade as lower ones, like wagon wheels that seem to spin backwards in old films. That is aliasing.

A 1 Hz tone sampled at 8 Hz is comfortable (Nyquist ok: yes); a 5 Hz tone at 8 Hz is not (no). Each sample is then quantised to one of 2ⁿ levels, so the bit rate = fs·n (here 24 b/s) and SNR ≈ 6.02n + 1.76 dB, which is 19.82 dB for 3 bits. In the figures, blue dots are samples and green are the quantised values, and the under-sampled tone is misread as a slower one. Sampling a 5 kHz tone at 8 kHz causes aliasing.

questions.prompt: Sampling a 5 kHz tone at 8 kHz causes…

choices.text: Aliasing — it appears as a 3 kHz tone.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Below Nyquist it is a problem.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: fs is below the Nyquist rate 2 × 5 = 10 kHz.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: The damage is to the frequency itself.

figures.note: Blue dots are samples; green are the quantised values.

keynotes: Sample at least twice per cycle of the highest frequency (fs ≥ 2 fmax), otherwise aliasing makes high frequencies look low.
A 1 Hz tone sampled at 8 Hz is fine; a 5 Hz tone at 8 Hz is not.
Each sample is quantised to one of 2ⁿ levels: rate = fs·n (24 b/s) and SNR ≈ 6.02n + 1.76 dB, which is 19.82 dB for 3 bits.

sections.title: Impairments
sections.body:
Signals never arrive as they left, as you will soon see. Three villains spoil them. Attenuation: the signal weakens with distance, measured in dB. Distortion: different frequencies travel at different speeds, smearing the pulses. And noise: thermal, crosstalk, impulse.

Decibels have a handy rule: they add. A 3 dB loss halves the power, and 10 dB is a factor 10. A cable loses 2 dB/km over 15 km, so 2 × 15 = 30 dB. The power ratio = 10^(−30/10) = 0.001, so only one thousandth arrives, which is why amplifiers are needed. A −3 dB change in power means the power is halved.

worked.why: A cable loses 2 dB/km over 15 km.
Power ratio = 10^(−30/10) = 0.001: one thousandth arrives, so amplifiers are needed.

questions.prompt: A −3 dB change in power means…

keynotes: Three impairments: attenuation (weakening, in dB), distortion (frequencies travel at different speeds) and noise (thermal, crosstalk, impulse).
Decibels add: a 3 dB loss halves the power and 10 dB is a factor 10.
A cable losing 2 dB/km over 15 km loses 30 dB, so only one thousandth of the power arrives.
